## Average Typing Speed
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/average-typing-speed.html

The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. 45–60 WPM is good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. Test your own speed below, then compare it with the benchmarks.

## What is the average typing speed?
The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy - that is where most adults land without deliberate practice. A speed of 45–60 WPM is considered good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. The table below shows how typing speeds are usually classified.
Skill level | Speed (WPM) | What it means
Beginner | Under 30 WPM | Still learning; hunt-and-peck on many keys
Below average | 30-45 WPM | Functional but slow; typing takes conscious effort
Average | 40-50 WPM | Where most adults land without practice
Good / above average | 60-80 WPM | Comfortable; meets most office job requirements
Fast | 80-100 WPM | Top ~10% of typists
Advanced / elite | 100+ WPM | Top ~1%; only about 1% type over 100 WPM
## Average typing speed by age
Typing speed is shaped more by how long someone has typed daily than by age itself, but it does follow a rough curve: it climbs through the teens, peaks in the late teens to twenties, then eases slightly later in life. These are approximate averages.
Age group | Average WPM | Notes
Under 13 | 15-30 WPM | Still building muscle memory; wide variance
13-18 | 35-55 WPM | Heavy phone users are often slower than expected
18-30 | 50-65 WPM | Peak learning years; fastest improvement
30-45 | 45-60 WPM | Stable; reflects accumulated work habits
45-60 | 40-55 WPM | Slight drop in raw speed, often higher accuracy
60+ | 30-45 WPM | Motor slowdown; practice still helps
## Typing speed by profession
Different jobs demand very different typing speeds. Roles where typing is the job - data entry, transcription, legal and executive support - expect well above average, while general office work is fine around 40–55 WPM. Accuracy usually matters as much as raw speed.
Job / role | Typing speed expected | Typical accuracy
General office work | 40-55 WPM | 95%+
Customer support / chat | 50-65 WPM | 97%+
Administrative assistant | 50-70 WPM | 97%+
Data entry | 60-80 WPM | 98%+
Medical transcription | 65-75 WPM | 98%+
Executive assistant | 70-80 WPM | 98%+
Legal secretary / paralegal | 70-90 WPM | 99%+
Benchmarks compiled from occupational typing data published by Wonderlic and TypingTest.now (2025-2026). Actual requirements vary by employer, test length, text and keyboard.
Want your own number? Take the typing speed test, measure it in characters per minute, or see the speeds employers require for jobs.
## How to type faster than average
If you are below the speed you want, the fastest way up is touch typing: use all ten fingers from the home row (ASDF JKL;) without looking at the keyboard. Prioritise accuracy over speed, practise 10–15 minutes a day, and keep your wrists relaxed. Most people add 10–20 WPM within a few weeks of daily practice.
## Benchmarks by age and goals
See also: average typing speed by age from kids to seniors, how many words per minute is fast, and the fastest typing speed records ever measured.
## Typing test FAQ
The average typing speed is about 40–50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. Most adults who have not practised deliberately settle between 40 and 60 WPM.
A good typing speed is 45–60 WPM. 60–80 WPM is above average and meets most office job requirements, while over 70 WPM is advanced. Only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM.
40 WPM is right around the adult average and is fine for everyday computer use. If you are accurate at 40 WPM, 60 WPM is a realistic next target with regular touch-typing practice.
On a normal QWERTY keyboard the fastest typists reach 150+ WPM. The highest reliably recorded speeds belong to Barbara Blackburn, who sustained 212 WPM on a Dvorak keyboard (a Guinness record), and Stella Pajunas, timed at 216 WPM back in 1946. Court reporters exceed 225 WPM, but on a specialised stenotype machine using shorthand chords, not a standard keyboard. For context the average is about 40 WPM, and professional typists aim for 97%+ accuracy.
Typing speed is measured in words per minute (WPM), where one word equals five characters including spaces. Net WPM subtracts errors, so WPM = (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes.
Touch type with all ten fingers from the home row (ASDF JKL;), prioritise accuracy over speed, and practise 10–15 minutes a day. Speed follows once your accuracy is consistently above 95%.

## CPM Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/cpm-typing-test.html

This CPM typing test measures your speed in characters per minute. CPM counts every correct keystroke, so because one word is five characters, CPM = WPM &times; 5. Type the passage below to see your live CPM, WPM and accuracy.

## What is CPM (characters per minute)?
CPM counts how many characters you type in one minute — every letter, number, space and symbol you produce. It is the rawest possible measure of typing output, which is why data-entry and transcription work quote speed in CPM or its hourly sibling KPH (keystrokes per hour) rather than in words.
On this site the conversion is the standard one used across the typing industry: five characters count as one word. So CPM is simply your WPM multiplied by five — no rounding tricks, no alternate formulas.
## WPM, CPM and KPH: the conversion table
Use this table to convert between the three units employers and exams quote. The formula is exact: CPM = WPM × 5, and KPH = CPM × 60.
WPM | CPM (WPM × 5) | KPH (CPM × 60)
20 | 100 | 6,000
30 | 150 | 9,000
40 | 200 | 12,000
50 | 250 | 15,000
60 | 300 | 18,000
80 | 400 | 24,000
100 | 500 | 30,000
120 | 600 | 36,000
Two reference points make the table easy to use: an average adult types about 40 WPM, which is 200 CPM or 12,000 KPH; the office-standard 60 WPM is 300 CPM or 18,000 KPH. Data-entry job postings asking for '8,000–10,000 KPH' are therefore asking for roughly 27–33 WPM — much less intimidating than the big number sounds.
## CPM vs WPM: which should you use?
Use WPM when you are comparing yourself with the classic typing benchmarks — schools, résumés and most online tests all quote it. Use CPM when the work itself is measured in keystrokes: numeric data entry, transcription, coding-adjacent tasks, and any language where 'word' is a fuzzy concept.
That last case matters more than it seems. In Japanese or Chinese, one character carries the meaning of a whole English word, so WPM understates the real work; CPM stays honest across scripts. The same is true for number-heavy documents, where a 'word' of five digits is far denser than a word of prose. If your job involves mixed text and figures, track both numbers for a week and see which one predicts your real output better.
## How this CPM test measures you
The timer starts on your first keystroke, and the live display tracks your character rate as you type. When the clock stops you get two figures: net CPM, which is your correct characters per minute with errors deducted at the standard weighting, and raw CPM, your gross keystroke rate before any penalty. The site uses the same five-characters-per-word standard across every page, so your CPM here converts directly to the WPM shown elsewhere with no second-guessing.
You also get the consistency score, which measures how even your keystroke timing is, and the per-key report showing which letters you miss and which ones slow you down. For character-rate work the slow-key list is gold: a single hesitant key — a bracket, a digit, a shifted symbol — taxes every word that contains it. Drill that one key and the whole character rate lifts.
Results save privately in your browser, building a history you can compare week to week. Because CPM is more granular than WPM, real progress shows up in the numbers sooner — a five-CPM gain is visible long before a one-WPM gain would be.
## The hidden cost of errors in CPM
Errors hurt twice in a character-based score. The mistyped character does not count, and the correction costs further keystrokes — a backspace and a retype at minimum, roughly two extra keystrokes for every mistake you actually fix. Unfixed errors are worse: they sit in the text and get deducted from your net figure at the end.
Run the arithmetic and the pattern is obvious. A raw 310 CPM at 94% accuracy nets below a controlled 290 CPM at 99%, and the cleaner run also produces better real documents. This is why every experienced data-entry trainer gives the same advice: find the speed where your accuracy stays above 97%, hold it until the character rate climbs on its own, then lift the ceiling a little. Accuracy is not the enemy of speed — it is the mechanism of it.
One more reason CPM deserves a place on your dashboard: it reacts to practice faster than WPM does. Because the unit is five times finer, a genuine improvement shows up as a visible CPM gain within days, while WPM might not tick over for weeks. That faster feedback loop keeps motivation honest — you can see the practice working, in keystrokes, almost as it happens.
## What is a good CPM typing speed?
Scaled from the standard WPM bands: around 200 CPM is the average adult, 300 CPM is good office-standard speed, 400 CPM is fast — the top ten percent — and 500 CPM or more is elite territory. The accuracy rule scales too: whatever your CPM, keep it above 97% accuracy, because every corrected error costs far more time than it saves.
WPM | CPM (= WPM × 5) | Level
20 WPM | 100 CPM | Beginner
40 WPM | 200 CPM | Average adult
60 WPM | 300 CPM | Good / office standard
80 WPM | 400 CPM | Fast
100 WPM | 500 CPM | Top ~1%
Watch your net figure, not the raw one. This test shows net CPM with errors deducted alongside your raw keystroke rate; the raw-minus-net gap is the clearest signal of whether you should push speed or tighten accuracy.
## How to raise your CPM
CPM rewards exactly one thing: more correct keystrokes per minute. Anything that removes hesitation raises it — home-row discipline, eyes on the screen, and drilling the specific keys your weak-key report flags after each round. Anything that creates backspaces lowers it, so type a touch slower than your panic speed and let accuracy do the compounding.
Symbols and digits carry more CPM weight than people expect, because they break letter rhythm. A few rounds in numbers or quotes mode each week keeps punctuation from collapsing your character rate. Short daily rounds on the 1 minute typing test build the base speed; then check the same run here to see it expressed in keystrokes.
## Drills that move your CPM
Different text types train different parts of your character rate. Numbers mode is the fastest way to raise digit-heavy CPM — the kind that data-entry and spreadsheet work actually measure. Quotes mode drills the punctuation and capitals that break letter rhythm in prose. Words mode strips away sentence flow and measures pure per-word burst speed, which is useful for diagnosing whether your ceiling is vocabulary or technique.
Structure the week around your weak-key report. Two or three 15-second sprints as a warm-up, one full minute for the measurement, then five minutes drilling whichever keys the report flagged. Alternate prose days with numbers days if your work involves figures. Once a week, take a longer run — three or five minutes — and watch how your character rate decays; stamina is trainable, and the decay curve flattening over weeks is the clearest sign of real progress.
## CPM and KPH benchmarks for jobs and exams
Data-entry job postings usually quote KPH — keystrokes per hour — with typical requirements between 8,000 and 12,000 KPH, plus an accuracy cutoff near 98%. Converted at the standard rate, that is roughly 130 to 200 CPM, or 27 to 40 WPM: demanding for a hunt-and-peck typist, comfortably reachable for anyone with a few weeks of touch-typing practice. Clerk, banking and court exams in several countries score short passages the same way, in keystrokes with an accuracy threshold.
Transcription and captioning sit higher, often expecting the equivalent of 300 CPM or more with near-perfect accuracy, because the work is continuous. Wherever a target is quoted in keystrokes, practise in CPM so the number on test day needs no mental conversion. Because this site uses the industry-standard five-character word, scores you measure here transfer directly to those requirements.
## CPM for data entry, exams and language typing
Data-entry employers quote KPH targets — typically 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — and exams for clerk and banking posts often score passages in keystrokes with an accuracy cutoff. Practising directly in CPM removes the mental conversion on test day. The keystrokes per hour test shows the same score in KPH, and the typing speed calculator converts any result between the three units instantly.
If you type in more than one language, CPM is also the only fair cross-language scoreboard: WPM shifts with each script's idea of a 'word', while characters are characters everywhere. The words per minute test page explains the word-based view in more detail.
## CPM for non-English and symbol-heavy typing
Words are a comfortable unit in English, but they get slippery elsewhere. Japanese and Chinese text has no spaces between words, so a 'word count' depends on a segmentation algorithm, not anything a typist can see. Agglutinative languages like Turkish or Finnish pack whole phrases into single long words, pushing WPM down even when finger speed is high. Code and data files invert the problem: brackets, operators and digits are dense with keystrokes but sparse with 'words'.
Characters never have this problem. A keystroke is a keystroke in every script and every file type, which is why CPM travels where WPM cannot: comparing your speed across languages, across prose and numbers, or across a week that mixed emails with spreadsheets. If you work in more than one language, CPM is the only scoreboard that treats them all fairly.
The same logic applies to accuracy. One mistyped character costs exactly one character of net score whether it sits in English prose, a Hindi conjunct or a line of figures — so the accuracy habits that raise your CPM transfer to every script you type.
## Typing test FAQ
CPM stands for characters per minute - the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is a finer-grained measure of typing speed than WPM.
Divide CPM by 5, because a word is defined as five characters. So 300 CPM equals 60 WPM and 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. To go the other way, WPM × 5 = CPM.

## Typing Practice for Programmers
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-practice-for-programmers.html

Programmers type a lot of symbols, brackets and camelCase &mdash; the exact characters most typing tests skip. Most developers type 50&ndash;70 WPM on prose, but what really matters is fluent symbols and a low error rate. Practise the way you code: paste your own code with custom text, or drill punctuation and numbers below.

## Why typing speed matters for programmers
A good typing speed for a programmer is 50-70 WPM, but coding is not a typing race - you spend far more time thinking than typing. Speed matters where it removes friction: the faster your fingers find brackets, operators and names, the less a thought is interrupted on its way to the screen. Accuracy matters even more, because a mistyped symbol is a syntax error you have to hunt down.
## What slows programmers down
Code is dense with characters that ordinary typing practice never covers - brackets, semicolons, operators, and numbers - plus naming styles like camelCase and snake_case that break your rhythm. The fix is to practise those specific characters, not more prose.
What you type in code | Why it is slow | Practise it here
Brackets & symbols () {} [] ; = > | Rare in word tests; awkward reaches for the pinkies | Punctuation test
Numbers & operators | Top row and keypad use different muscle memory | Number test
Your real code | camelCase, indentation and your stack&rsquo;s idioms | Custom text
## How to practise typing as a developer
Paste a real file you work in using custom text and type it for accuracy, not speed. Spend a few minutes on the punctuation and number drills so symbol reaches become automatic. Keep your fingers on the home row and let the weak pinkies own the bracket and semicolon keys. Ten focused minutes a day beats one long session.

## How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-to-type-without-looking.html

To type without looking, rest your fingers on the home row &mdash; left hand on ASDF, right hand on JKL; &mdash; feel the small bumps on F and J, and let each finger own its own keys. The skill is called touch typing, and it comes from short daily practice, not talent. Here is exactly how to build it, then test yourself below.

## Start on the home row (ASDF JKL;)
Put your left index finger on F and your right index finger on J - both have a raised bump so you can find them without looking. Your other fingers fall onto A S D and K L ; . This is &lsquo;home&rsquo;: every key is reached from here and your fingers return here between keystrokes. Each finger is responsible for the keys directly above and below its home key.
## Train muscle memory, not your eyes
The whole skill is not looking down. Keep your eyes on the screen, use the on-screen keyboard and hand guide below to see the next key, and resist peeking even when it feels slow at first. Practise 10-15 minutes a day and prioritise accuracy over speed - speed is just accurate muscle memory repeated. The touch typing test and the on-screen keyboard test highlight the next key and the correct finger as you go.
## How long until you can touch type?
Most people stop needing to look within a few weeks of daily practice, and return to their old speed within one to two months - faster after that, because touch typing has no ceiling the way hunt-and-peck does. Check your progress against the average typing speed as you go.
## Typing test FAQ
Rest your fingers on the home row (ASDF for the left hand, JKL; for the right), find the bumps on F and J by feel, keep your eyes on the screen, and let each finger own its keys. Practise a little every day.
Most people stop peeking within a few weeks of short daily practice, then take another month or two to match their old hunt-and-peck speed. Cover the keys and trust the F and J bumps to go faster.
A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. F and J have raised bumps so you can locate the home row without looking.
Looking down breaks your focus on the text and caps your speed. Typing by feel keeps your eyes on the screen and lets muscle memory take over, which is faster and more accurate.
Yes. Touch typing is muscle memory, not talent or age — short, consistent daily practice works at any age.

## Colemak Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/colemak-typing.html

Use the QWERTY / Dvorak / Colemak switch in the keyboard toolbar any time. Switch your operating system to Colemak, take the test, and get WPM, accuracy and consistency.

## colemak typing test
Most typing tests only draw a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless for Colemak typing practice: the label you are hunting for is not on the key you press. This test flips the on-screen keyboard to the Colemak layout, keeping the physical QWERTY key positions and relabelling every key, so the finger guide on screen matches exactly what a Colemak typist sees.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system. The page only draws the Colemak keyboard; you switch your operating system input to Colemak, start typing, and the test scores the characters your layout produces - so your WPM, accuracy, consistency and the per-key heatmap are all measured for real Colemak typing.
## Why Colemak
Colemak was published in 2006 as a middle path between QWERTY and Dvorak. It keeps the common shortcut keys Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places and changes only 17 keys, so the switch is far gentler than Dvorak while still putting the most-used letters under your fingers.
On the same English passage, Colemak keeps about 73% of letters on the home row (QWERTY is near 36%) and cuts repeated same-finger presses to roughly 1.5%, versus about 7.9% on QWERTY. Less finger travel usually means more comfort over long sessions; it does not guarantee a higher top speed, which still depends mostly on practice.
## How to practice Colemak typing
Set your operating system input to Colemak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY characters while looking at a Colemak keyboard. Start with short two-to-five minute sessions and resist looking at your hands - the finger guide and on-screen keyboard exist to replace that habit.
Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week or two; that is the switch cost, not a verdict on Colemak. Track accuracy here before speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it. Compare Colemak with Dvorak and QWERTY on the keyboard layouts page.

## Keyboard Layouts Compared
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-layouts.html

QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Workman compared on home-row use, finger travel and same-finger presses &mdash; so you can see which keyboard layout fits you before you commit weeks to switching. Try any of them on the test below with a layout-matched on-screen keyboard and finger guide.

## QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman
A keyboard layout is just the map of which letter sits under each key. QWERTY has been the default since the 1870s, but alternative layouts rearrange the letters so the most common ones sit on the home row, cutting finger travel. Here is how the four best-known layouts compare on the same English text.
Layout | Introduced | Finger travel* | Home-row use | Same-finger
QWERTY | 1870s | 153 m (baseline) | 36% | 7.9%
Dvorak | 1936 | 88 m (&minus;42%) | 71% | 3.2%
Colemak | 2006 | 89 m (&minus;42%) | 73% | 1.5%
Workman | 2010 | 84 m (&minus;45%) | 67% | 2.0%
*Modeled finger travel for the same 5,847-character English passage on a standard keyboard, with the share of letters typed without leaving the home row and the share of consecutive keys pressed by the same finger. Figures from the Typing Cat layout comparison lab; they are estimates of movement, not measured typing speeds.
## Which keyboard layout is best?
There is no single best layout, because less finger movement is not the same as faster typing. QWERTY wins on familiarity: it is on every shared computer and every shortcut assumes it. Dvorak alternates hands the most (about 67% of keystrokes), which many typists find rhythmic for long English prose. Colemak keeps the most letters on the home row (73%) and the fewest awkward same-finger presses (1.5%) while leaving Z, X, C, V and most shortcuts in place, so it is the usual pick for QWERTY users who want to switch. Workman trims total finger travel the most by also minimising sideways stretches.
For almost everyone, practice and accuracy move your WPM far more than the layout does. A fast QWERTY typist will beat a beginner on any layout. Switch for comfort and reduced finger travel, not for a guaranteed speed jump.
## Should you switch keyboard layout?
Switching costs you one to four weeks of slower, deliberate typing while new muscle memory forms, and shared or public machines will still be QWERTY. The payoff is less finger travel and, for many people, more comfort in long sessions. It is worth it mainly if you type a lot of English every day and own the keyboards you use most.
If you want the gentlest change, start with Colemak because it keeps your common shortcuts. If you love hand-alternation, try Dvorak. The honest answer for casual typists is that staying on QWERTY and practising is the higher-return move.
## Try each keyboard layout here
You can practise two of these layouts right now with a matching on-screen keyboard and finger guide: take the Colemak typing test or the Dvorak typing test, or measure your current speed on QWERTY with the main typing speed test. Each shows WPM, accuracy, consistency and a per-key heatmap so you can compare how a layout feels for you.
## Choosing a layout
Layout decisions: Dvorak vs QWERTY — evidence, retraining cost, and who should switch.
## Keyboard layouts FAQ
No layout is reliably fastest for everyone. Modeling shows Dvorak, Colemak and Workman cut finger travel by roughly 42 to 45% versus QWERTY, but measured typing speed depends far more on practice and accuracy than on the layout. The world's fastest typists use several different layouts, including QWERTY.
Dvorak puts about 71% of letters on the home row versus QWERTY's 36% and alternates hands more, which many typists find more comfortable for long English text. Studies show modest speed gains at best, so the main benefit is reduced finger movement and comfort, not a guaranteed speed jump.
Colemak keeps more letters on the home row (about 73%) and the lowest same-finger rate (about 1.5%), and it changes only 17 keys while keeping Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places, so it is easier to switch to than Dvorak. Dvorak alternates hands more. Which feels better is personal.
Code uses far more punctuation, brackets and symbols than English prose, so prose-optimised layouts help less. Programmer variants such as Programmer Dvorak and Workman Programmer rearrange the number and symbol rows. Many developers stay on QWERTY because editors, shortcuts and pair-programming all assume it.
Most people reach usable speed again in one to four weeks of short daily practice, and return to their old speed over one to three months. Accuracy recovers before raw speed, so track accuracy first.
Yes. This site has a free Dvorak typing test and a free Colemak typing test, each with an on-screen keyboard relabelled to that layout and a matching finger guide, so you can practise and measure your WPM without installing anything.

## 10 Key Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ten-key-typing-test.html

A 10 key typing test measures how fast you type on the numeric keypad &mdash; the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard &mdash; using the fingers of your right hand. It is the standard speed test for data entry, accounting and finance work. Take the timed number-pad test below and get your speed instantly.

## What is a 10 key typing test?
10 key typing (also written ten key typing or 10-key) is touch typing on the numeric keypad: the number, arithmetic and Enter keys on the right of a full-size keyboard. Instead of hunting for digits across the top row, a 10 key typist keeps the right hand anchored on 4 5 6 with the index, middle and ring fingers, and reaches every other key from there. It is the skill behind fast data entry, bookkeeping and banking work.
This page runs a numpad typing test in numbers mode, so the practice text is digits, decimals, dates and amounts - exactly the characters a 10 key operator types all day. Switch the Time chips to 15 or 30 seconds for a quick check, or run 3-5 minutes for a stable result.
## The 10 key home row (4 5 6)
Rest your index finger on 4, your middle finger on 5 and your ring finger on 6 - these three usually have a raised bump or a dot so you can find them without looking. The index finger also covers 1 and 7, the middle covers 2 and 8, the ring covers 3 and 9, and the little finger handles 0, . and Enter. Your thumb rests on the 0 key on many layouts.
The golden rule of ten key typing is the same as touch typing on the letter keys: eyes on the screen, fingers always returning to 4 5 6 between digits. Speed comes from never looking down.
## How is 10 key speed measured?
10 key speed is usually quoted in keystrokes per hour (KPH) or characters per minute (CPM), not words per minute. A comfortable 10 key speed for data entry is about 8,000-10,000 KPH (roughly 130-165 CPM), and strong operators reach 12,000-15,000 KPH with 99%+ accuracy.
Level | 10 key speed
Beginner | 3,000-5,000 KPH
Average | 5,000-8,000 KPH
Data entry ready | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Fast / professional | 12,000-15,000+ KPH
This test reports your characters per minute live; multiply by 60 to get an approximate keystrokes-per-hour figure, or use the dedicated keystrokes per hour test.
## Why practise the number pad separately?
The top number row and the numeric keypad use completely different muscle memory. Typing letters fast does not make you fast at the number pad, and many people lose a data entry job interview on the 10 key portion alone. Practising the numpad on its own trains the right hand to hit 0-9 and the decimal point without a single glance at the keyboard.
If you need both, warm up with this 10 key typing test and then check your general speed on the number typing test or the main typing speed test.
## 10 key typing FAQ
A 10 key typing test measures how quickly you type on the numeric keypad (the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard) using your right hand, keeping the fingers anchored on the 4, 5 and 6 keys.
For data entry work, aim for at least 8,000 keystrokes per hour (about 133 characters per minute). Experienced operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy or better.
It is touch typing applied to the numeric keypad. You keep your eyes on the screen, rest the fingers on 4 5 6, and let each finger own its column of digits.
Practise a few minutes a day with your eyes off the keyboard, keep the index, middle and ring fingers on 4, 5 and 6, and prioritise accuracy - errors cost more time than a slightly slower but clean run.
On laptops with no dedicated keypad you can use an external USB numeric keypad, or practise the digits with the number-typing mode instead, which uses the top number row.

## Data Entry Typing Test

A data entry typing test checks the two things employers screen for: typing speed and accuracy. Data entry roles typically ask for 50&ndash;70 WPM (or 8,000&ndash;10,000 keystrokes per hour) with 97&ndash;99% accuracy. Take the timed test below and see where you stand.

## What speed does data entry require?
Data entry and clerical jobs usually expect 50-70 WPM with 97%+ accuracy. Numeric-heavy roles are often measured in keystrokes per hour instead, where the bar is about 8,000-10,000 KPH. Some employers use a 10 key (numeric keypad) test rather than a text passage.
Metric | Typical data entry requirement

Accuracy | 97-99%
Numeric (10 key) | 8,000-10,000 KPH
Test length | 1-5 minutes
Benchmarks reflect commonly published data entry job requirements; actual figures vary by employer.
## Accuracy matters more than raw speed
In data entry, a wrong digit is worse than a slow one, so most employers score net speed - your speed after errors are subtracted - and many set a hard accuracy floor. Practise typing clean the first time rather than relying on backspace, and let speed rise on its own as the keystrokes become automatic.
Take the test at the length the employer uses. Most screening tests run 1 to 5 minutes, so warm up with a 1 minute test and then do a 3 minute or 5 minute run.
## How to prepare for a data entry typing test
Practise with real text that includes numbers, punctuation and capitals, because that is what the passage will contain - not a clean word list. If the role is numeric, train the number pad separately with the 10 key typing test. Sit comfortably, keep your fingers on the home row, and do two or three warm-up runs before your scored attempt so you are at your normal speed.
Every result here is saved in your browser, so you can watch both WPM and accuracy improve over the days before an interview. Your history is private and stays on your device.

Most data-entry postings quote 8,000–12,000 keystrokes per hour with ~98% accuracy — about 27–40 WPM — and professional numeric roles can reach 12,000–15,000 KPH. For the full requirements table across every scenario, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

## Keystrokes Per Hour Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keystrokes-per-hour-test.html

A keystrokes per hour (KPH) test measures typing speed the way many data entry employers do &mdash; in keystrokes over an hour, not words per minute. Data entry roles commonly require 8,000&ndash;10,000 KPH. Type the passage below and convert your result to KPH instantly.

## What is keystrokes per hour?
Keystrokes per hour (KPH or KSPH) counts how many individual key presses you make in an hour, counting every character including spaces. It is the standard measure for data entry and numeric keypad work because it does not depend on how long the words happen to be. A fast data entry operator reaches 10,000-15,000 KPH.
If you know your characters per minute (CPM), multiply by 60 to get KPH: a steady 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH. This test shows your characters per minute live, so you can read your KPH straight off the result.
## KPH vs WPM vs CPM
All three describe the same typing, just at different scales. WPM counts words (5 characters each) per minute; CPM counts characters per minute; KPH counts keystrokes per hour. Because a &lsquo;word&rsquo; is standardised as 5 characters, the conversions are fixed:
Your speed | WPM | CPM | KPH
Average | 40 | 200 | 12,000
Good | 60 | 300 | 18,000
Fast | 80 | 400 | 24,000
Elite | 100 | 500 | 30,000
The table assumes no error penalty; employers usually apply a net-accuracy penalty, so your effective KPH is lower than the raw figure.
## What KPH do data entry jobs require?
Job postings for data entry and clerical work often ask for 8,000-10,000 KPH with a high accuracy rate; some set the bar at 12,000 KPH. Numeric roles may test the number pad specifically, so pair this test with the 10 key typing test. Measure your text speed here and your WPM on the words per minute test, then check the requirements in the typing test for jobs page.
## How do KPH requirements convert to WPM?
Divide by 300: WPM = KPH ÷ 300, so a 10,000 KPH posting is asking for about 33 WPM. For the complete table of KPH, CPM and WPM requirements by job and exam, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.
## Where KPH scores lead

For data entry work, 8,000 to 10,000 KPH is the usual requirement, and fast operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy. General office roles often accept lower KPH because typing is only part of the job.
WPM = KPH ÷ 300. Because 1 word is 5 characters and there are 60 minutes in an hour, 60 WPM equals 18,000 KPH.

## Typing Speed Calculator
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-calculator.html

This typing speed calculator tells you how your typing speed converts between WPM (words per minute), CPM (characters per minute) and KPH (keystrokes per hour). Measure your real speed with the test below, then use the formulas and table to convert any figure. Everything runs in your browser.

## How to calculate typing speed (WPM)
Typing speed in words per minute (WPM) is worked out with one simple formula: WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Every five characters count as one &lsquo;word&rsquo;, so longer words are worth more. Net WPM subtracts your errors first: net WPM = ((correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes). Employers use net WPM, because a mistake you have to fix costs time.
To get your own numbers, just take the timed test above - it computes WPM, raw WPM, CPM and accuracy for you, so you can read your result straight off the scoreboard.
## WPM, CPM and KPH conversions
The three common typing-speed units are all fixed multiples of each other, so you can convert any of them by hand:
From | To | Formula
CPM | WPM | WPM = CPM ÷ 5
WPM | CPM | CPM = WPM × 5
CPM | KPH | KPH = CPM × 60
WPM | KPH | KPH = WPM × 300
WPM | | WPM = (characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes
So 60 WPM = 300 CPM = 18,000 KPH. These are the standard conversions used by typing certificates and data entry employers.
## Worked examples
If you type 300 characters in 1 minute, that is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 WPM (or 18,000 KPH). If you type 1,200 characters in 3 minutes, that is (1,200 ÷ 5) ÷ 3 = 80 WPM. If you make 12 mistakes over that run, your net speed is (1,200 &minus; 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 3 = 79 WPM.
Want the measured number instead of the maths? Run the words per minute test for WPM, the CPM typing test for characters per minute, or the keystrokes per hour test for KPH.
## Typing speed calculator FAQ
WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes elapsed. Every 5 characters count as one word, so 300 characters in 1 minute is 60 WPM.
Divide characters per minute by 5. So 250 CPM is 50 WPM, and 400 CPM is 80 WPM.
Multiply WPM by 300. For example, 60 WPM equals 18,000 keystrokes per hour.
Gross WPM counts every character you typed; net WPM subtracts your errors first. Employers almost always use net WPM because it reflects usable output.
Yes. The typing speed calculator and every typing test on this site are completely free, with no sign-up and no account.

## Quick Brown Fox Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/quick-brown-fox-typing-test.html

The &lsquo;the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; sentence is the most famous pangram in typing practice &mdash; a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. Typing it is the traditional warm-up and a quick way to check that every key on your keyboard works. Take the test below and measure your speed and accuracy.

## What is the quick brown fox sentence?
&lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; is a pangram: a sentence that uses all 26 letters of the alphabet at least once. Because it covers the whole keyboard it has been the standard typing drill for over a century, and it is still used to test typewriters, keyboards and fonts. Practising it warms up every finger before a longer typing test.
Type it a few times here - the test scrolls through alphabet-rich sentences in the same spirit, so your warm-up trains every letter rather than only the common ones.
## Why practise with pangrams?
Ordinary sentences repeat the same handful of common letters and rarely touch q, z, x or j. A pangram forces every key into the run, which is exactly what you need before a speed attempt: it surfaces the awkward keys while the stakes are low. That is why &lsquo;quick brown fox&rsquo; games appear in almost every typing tutor and school typing class.
For a targeted version, the keyboard typing test highlights the next key and the correct finger, and the easy typing test uses simple high-frequency words if the pangram still feels hard.
## Quick brown fox and keyboard checking
Because the pangram contains every letter, typing it is the fastest way to confirm that no key is broken or stuck: if a letter is missing from the output, that key is faulty. Try it with capitals and punctuation too - &lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.&rsquo; - to exercise the shift keys and the full stop. Then move on to a full typing speed test to get your WPM.
## Quick brown fox FAQ
&lsquo;The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog&rsquo; is a pangram - a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. It has been the classic typing-practice sentence for over a century.
Because it uses all 26 letters, it exercises every key and finger in one short line, making it an ideal warm-up and a fast way to check that your keyboard works.
It is a good warm-up, but the unusual letters (q, z, x) make it harder than common-word practice. Beginners may prefer the easy typing test first.
The classic sentence is nine words: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. It contains 35 letters.
Yes. If a letter is missing from what you type, that key is faulty. Include the full stop and capitals to test shift and punctuation keys as well.

## Home Row Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/home-row-typing-test.html

The home row is the row of keys your fingers rest on &mdash; A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right. Every key on the keyboard is reached from here, which is why home-row practice is the first lesson in touch typing. Take the timed test below to drill the home row and track your progress.

## What is the home row?
The home row (also called the home keys) is the middle row of the keyboard where your fingers rest between keystrokes: A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right hand. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so your index fingers can find home by feel alone, without looking down.
Home-row typing is the foundation of touch typing. Each finger owns a column of keys and always returns to its home key, so the hand never has to hunt for a letter. Start by typing only home-row letters until they feel automatic, then add the rows above and below.
## Which finger types which home key?
Home key | Finger | Also reaches
A | Left pinky | Q, Z, 1
S | Left ring | W, X, 2
D | Left middle | E, C, 3
F | Left index | R, T, G, V, B, 4, 5
J | Right index | Y, U, H, N, M, 6, 7
K | Right middle | I, comma, 8
L | Right ring | O, full stop, 9
; | Right pinky | P, slash, 0
The thumbs rest on the space bar. Keeping this assignment is what lets you type without looking - see the full method on how to type without looking.
## Home row drills and practice
Effective home-row practice repeats the eight home keys in short, varied bursts rather than long paragraphs, so your fingers build the exact movements they need. Run this test for 1 or 2 minutes a day, aiming first for perfect accuracy and only then for speed. When the home row feels natural, move on to the touch typing test and the keyboard typing test, which introduce the surrounding rows with an on-screen finger guide.
## Hand and finger fundamentals
Placement done right: proper hand position for typing and the typing finger chart.
## Home row FAQ
A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right hand, with the thumbs on the space bar. F and J have raised bumps so you can find the row without looking.
It is the base position of touch typing. Every key is reached from home and the fingers return there, so you never have to look down to find a letter.
Left hand: pinky on A, ring on S, middle on D, index on F. Right hand: index on J, middle on K, ring on L, pinky on ;.
Most people feel comfortable within a few days of short daily practice, but full touch typing across all rows takes a few weeks of consistent practice.
No. Keep your eyes on the screen and use the F and J bumps to find home. Looking down slows the muscle memory you are trying to build.

## What is a good typing speed for an adult?
The average adult typing speed is about 40 WPM. Reaching 60 WPM puts you comfortably above average and is enough for most office work; 80 WPM is fast, and 100 WPM+ is top-tier. Age or when you learned to type matter far less than how much you practise.
Adult typing level | WPM
Below average | under 35
Average | 40-50
Good (office standard) | 60-80
Fast | 80-100
Elite (top ~1%) | 100+
These bands come from published typing-speed studies; see the full average typing speed breakdown by age and profession.
## You can still learn to type faster as an adult
It is a common myth that only children can build typing speed. Adults usually improve faster than children because they follow instructions, understand why accuracy comes before speed and can practise deliberately. The catch is unlearning years of two-finger habit: the fix is to slow down, keep the fingers on the home row, and look at the screen instead of the keyboard.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough. Start with the home row typing test, then the touch typing test, and only push for raw speed once your accuracy is steady.

## Typing Skill Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-skill-test.html

A typing skill test tells you how good you are at typing: your words per minute (WPM), your accuracy and your error rate, combined into one clear picture of your typing skill level. It is the same kind of test used for job applications and typing exams. Take it below and get your score instantly.

## What is a typing skill test?
A typing skill test (also called a typing skills test or typing proficiency test) measures how fast and how accurately you can type a passage. You are timed, and your result is reported as WPM plus an accuracy percentage and an error count. Employers, schools and government exams use this format to compare candidates objectively.
Unlike a plain speed test, a skill test is judged on the combination of speed and accuracy. 70 WPM at 90% accuracy is a weaker result than 60 WPM at 99%, because the errors have to be fixed and cost real time.
## What counts as a good typing skill score?
Skill level | WPM | Accuracy
Beginner | under 30 | under 90%
Basic | 30-40 | 90-95%
Proficient | 40-60 | 95-98%
Advanced | 60-80 | 98-99%
Expert | 80+ | 99%+
For most office jobs, 50-60 WPM with 97%+ accuracy is expected. For data entry, exams and specialised roles the bar is higher - see the typing test for jobs requirements.
## How to improve your typing skill score
Improvement comes from accuracy first, speed second. Slow down until you can type a full minute without errors, keep the fingers on the home row, and look at the screen rather than the keyboard. Practise daily for ten to fifteen minutes, mixing a general typing practice run with a targeted accuracy test. Boost weak spots with the weak-key drill, and check your standing against the average typing speed.
## Typing skill test FAQ

Prioritise accuracy, keep your fingers on the home row, look at the screen, and practise a short session every day rather than a long one occasionally.

## Paragraph Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/paragraph-typing-test.html

Practise with full paragraphs instead of single words — the format real typing exams and job tests use.

## Paragraph vs word typing test
A word test flashes a list of common words, which rewards pure finger speed. A paragraph typing test gives you connected sentences with spaces, capitals and punctuation — closer to what you actually type at work, and to what most exams and employers set.
## Why paragraphs are harder
Paragraphs make you hold rhythm across long familiar phrases, returning to the home row for capitals and reaching for the comma and full stop without breaking flow. Because the text is real language, you also cannot autopilot a short list of repeated words — you have to read ahead.
## Choose your passage length
Use the timer chips to sit a 1-minute paragraph for a quick check, a 5-minute paragraph for practice, or a 10-minute paragraph for full exam stamina. Longer passages expose the speed decay that short bursts hide.
## How to use this page
Start typing and keep going until the timer runs out. Your WPM, accuracy and a per-second speed chart appear straight away. Practise two or three passages a day and review where your accuracy drops — that is where the lost words per minute hide.
## Paragraph Typing Test FAQ
It is a typing test where you copy a full passage of connected sentences rather than a list of single words, so capitals, spaces and punctuation count just as they do in real writing.
Exam passages are usually 300 to 500 words. On this page you choose 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 minutes so you can practise the exact length your exam or employer uses.
Yes. Real sentences add capitals, punctuation and reading ahead, so scores are typically a little lower than a pure word-list test — but far closer to your true working speed.

## A friendly first test
Most typing tests throw long words and heavy punctuation at you from the first keystroke. This beginner version keeps the text short and the words common, so you can finish a passage and actually see a score instead of drowning in errors.
## Where should a beginner start?
Begin with the home row — A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. Learn to reach each key with the correct finger instead of hunting with two fingers, even if it feels slower for the first few days. Speed is a by-product of accuracy; accuracy is a by-product of good technique.
## Don't chase speed yet

## Timed Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/timed-typing-test.html

A ticking clock is the fairest way to measure typing speed. Choose your length and see how many words you can type before the buzzer.

## How a timed typing test works
You type for a fixed number of seconds or minutes and the test counts every correctly typed character, then converts it to words per minute. Because the clock never pauses for backspacing, a timed test rewards clean, steady typing over burst speed.
## Pick the right duration
Careers and most online tests use one minute, so a 1-minute timed test is the standard benchmark. Data-entry and government exams often run three or five minutes to test stamina. Sprint-style challenges use 15 or 30 seconds, and typing-race communities favour 10 minutes to expose who holds speed under fatigue.
## Why timing matters
Without a clock it is easy to slow down on hard words or rest on your laurels. A timer forces an even rhythm and gives you a number you can compare week to week — the only way to know whether your practice is actually working.
## Beat your own clock
Start shorter than you think you need: a 30-second timed test you finish cleanly teaches more than a 10-minute slog full of errors. Once you hold your accuracy above 97%, extend the duration and watch net speed stay flat — that is real progress.
## Timed Typing Test FAQ
A typing test where you type against a countdown clock for a set duration — usually 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 minutes — and your speed is measured in words per minute.
One minute is the most common, used by most online tests and employers. Career exams and government tests often use three to five minutes.
No. The clock keeps running so the score reflects your true working speed, including any slowdown caused by corrections.
Yes — use the duration chips to pick anything from 15 seconds to 10 minutes.

## Fast Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/fast-typing-test.html

Already comfortable on the keyboard? Measure just how fast you really are — and find the ceiling you can push past.

## What counts as fast typing?
The average person types around 40 words per minute. Above 60 WPM you are quicker than most people you will meet, and 80 WPM or more puts you in the top few percent of typists. Professional transcriptionists and programmers often sit between 80 and 120 WPM.
## Why some people type faster
Fast typists are not just fast — they are accurate. They touch type all ten fingers on the home row, keep their hands anchored, and read a few words ahead so their eyes never stall on a hard word. Raw finger speed matters far less than never breaking rhythm.
## Push past your plateau
Once you are fast, big gains come from fixing the few keys that cost you time. Turn on the on-screen keyboard highlight and notice which letters make you hesitate — then drill those. A single problem key fixed can add several words per minute.
## Test under pressure
A fast typing test is also a pressure test. Type for one minute at maximum effort, then look at the accuracy figure: if it dropped below 90%, you are typing beyond your control and would score higher by easing off slightly.
## Fast Typing Test FAQ
Anything above 60 words per minute is fast for a general typist. 80 WPM or more is top-tier, and professional typists often reach 100 to 120 WPM.
The all-time English record is above 200 words per minute, but that is a specialised achievement. For everyday users, 80 to 100 WPM already puts you in the top 1%.

## Hard Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/hard-typing-test.html

Easy text hides weak fingers. This hard test adds capitals, symbols and numbers so every part of the keyboard gets a workout.

## Why the text is harder
Real documents are not lists of clean short words. They contain capital letters, commas, apostrophes, dashes, numbers and long multi-syllable words. This hard test mixes all of them so you practise the reaches that a simple word test never touches.
## What a hard test exposes
A sudden shift to a capital sends your hand away from the home row; a number row stretch breaks your rhythm; heavy punctuation makes you hunt for a key you rarely use. Those are exactly the moments where speed and accuracy leak away in real work.
## How to score well on hard text
Slow your overall rate just enough to keep accuracy high, and use the correct fingers even for the awkward keys — the number row and both little fingers are the usual weak spots. Practising hard text on purpose is how easy text becomes effortless.
## When to step up to hard mode
If you already hold 90%+ accuracy on normal passages and want to keep improving, hard mixed text is your next challenge. Expect your WPM to dip at first; that is the point — you are training new reaches, and speed returns higher.
## Hard Typing Test FAQ
Difficult tests include capital letters, numbers, symbols, uncommon words and punctuation, forcing reaches far from the home row instead of simple repeated words.
Because your hand has to leave the home row for capitals and the number row, and unusual words slow your reading ahead. A lower score on hard text is normal.
Yes, if you already type normal text accurately. Hard passages train the reaches that ordinary practice ignores, which raises your ceiling.
Yes, free and with no sign-up.

## Advanced Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/advanced-typing-test.html

For people who already type well: a demanding passage and honest scoring to see whether you belong in the top percentile.

## Built for experienced typists
If you already clear 60 WPM comfortably, an easy test tells you nothing. This advanced test uses longer, richer passages and expects full command of capitals, punctuation and the number row — a genuine stretch for a practised touch typist.
## Targets for advanced typists
Professional transcriptionists, programmers and typists working from dictation live between 80 and 120 WPM. An advanced target is 80 WPM or more at 98% accuracy; anything above 100 WPM is elite and rare.
## Where advanced speed is really won
At this level you are not limited by finger speed but by attention: reading far ahead, holding rhythm through difficult phrases, and never looking at your hands. Small reductions in hesitation, not faster fingers, are what move an advanced score upward.
## Use it as a true benchmark
Take this test monthly and record your net WPM. Because the passages are demanding and consistent, a rising score here is a far better signal of genuine progress than a lucky 10-second sprint.

## How Fast Can I Type?
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/how-fast-can-i-type.html

One minute is all it takes to answer the question. Type the passage and get your words per minute and accuracy instantly.

## Find your words per minute
Words per minute, or WPM, is the standard measure of typing speed. It is calculated from the number of correctly typed characters divided by five — the average length of an English word — over the time you typed. This page gives you a clean one-minute reading.
## How you compare
The average adult types around 40 WPM. Under 30 WPM is below average, 40 to 60 WPM is exactly average to comfortable, 60 to 80 WPM is fast, and above 100 WPM is rare and professional-level. These figures are for typing on a keyboard in your own language.
## What your score really means
Speed without accuracy is misleading. A 70 WPM score at 88% accuracy is worth less than 55 WPM at 99%, because in real typing you have to fix every error. Always read the two numbers together.
## Can you type faster?
Almost certainly yes. Almost everyone can gain ten to twenty words per minute by learning to touch type with all ten fingers and by drilling the specific keys that make them hesitate. Ten focused minutes a day is enough.
## How Fast Can I Type FAQ
The average adult types about 40 words per minute. Anything above 60 WPM is considered fast and 80 WPM or more is top-tier.
In words per minute, where one word equals five typed characters. Your WPM is the correct characters divided by five, per minute.
Take the one-minute test on this page — it gives you your exact words-per-minute score plus an accuracy percentage in sixty seconds.
Yes: learn to touch type with all ten fingers, keep accuracy above 97%, and practise deliberately for about ten minutes a day. Most people can add 10 to 20 WPM.

## Typing Test for Interview
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-test-for-interview.html

Employers often ask you to sit a typing test before or during an interview. Rehearse the exact format here so there are no surprises on the day.

## Why employers test typing at interviews
A typing test gives a fast, objective reading of a candidate's real ability. Rather than trusting a CV claim, recruiters sit you at a keyboard, start a clock and watch the score — usually one to three minutes of ordinary business text with capitals and punctuation.
## What employers expect
Admin, customer-service and support roles typically ask for 40 to 55 WPM with 95% or higher accuracy. Data-entry and transcription roles push to 60 to 70 WPM, or measure keystrokes per hour for numeric work. Government and legal positions often add a formal minimum that you must clear to qualify at all.
## Rehearse the real thing
Use the timer to simulate the exact length your employer uses, and type business-style passages rather than clean word lists. Practise proofreading on the fly: many tests mark you down for uncorrected errors, so type a little slower and cleaner than you can.
## Turn nerves into an advantage
Interview pressure costs most candidates five to ten WPM. Because you have practised the format here, the test itself will feel routine — that calm alone is often worth several words per minute.
## Interview test strategy
Pass the interview round: how to pass a typing test with test-day protocol, and typing test tips for before, during and after.
## Interview Typing Test FAQ
Many do, especially for administrative, data-entry, customer-service and secretarial roles. It is usually a short timed test of one to three minutes.
Most administrative roles ask for 40 to 55 WPM with 95%+ accuracy. Data-entry and transcription roles often want 60 to 70 WPM.
Practise timed one to three-minute tests on business-style passages, keep accuracy above 95%, and rehearse typing cleanly under mild pressure.

## Bank Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/bank-typing-test.html

Banking and clerical exams often include a typing round with a strict accuracy cut-off. Practise the format and the pace here.

## Typing in banking exams
Many bank clerk and clerical recruitment exams include a typing test as a qualifying round: you must reach a set speed and accuracy, and failing it can end your application regardless of your written score. The format is a timed passage, usually in the language you applied in, with accuracy checked closely.
## The usual standard
Common requirements sit around 30 to 40 words per minute with at least 90% accuracy, and many boards set a hard floor on errors — a fixed number of mistakes is allowed and no more. Because the pass mark is about accuracy, clean typing beats raw speed.
## Passages and language
Bank typing rounds use ordinary prose, not technical jargon, but they are timed strictly and often use a fixed paragraph you cannot choose. Practise on uninterrupted passages of a few hundred words and get used to holding focus without fixing every tiny slip.
## How to practise
Set the timer to match your exam — often five minutes — and aim to finish comfortably under the error limit before you try to raise speed. Once you can pass at 97% accuracy, push your WPM up in small steps. Watch our data entry and government typing pages for the same family of clerical tests.
## What typing speed do bank exams require?
Bank clerk typing tests typically ask for short timed passages in the 25–35 WPM range with an accuracy threshold. For the full table of requirements across data entry, clerk, government and office scenarios, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

## SSC Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/ssc-typing-test.html

SSC typing rounds are a qualifying stage with a strict speed and accuracy bar. Practise the format here before the real thing.

## What the SSC typing test is
Several SSC recruitment exams include a typing test as a qualifying round, typically typing a passage in a set time to prove a minimum speed and accuracy. It is often held at a test centre and must be cleared to be considered for the post, no matter how well you did in the written exam.
## The usual requirement
SSC typing rounds commonly ask for around 35 words per minute in English, or roughly 30 words per minute in Hindi, with high accuracy. Some exams set the bar in a mix of speed and error count, so you must meet both to pass.
## Training for the format
The passage is delivered on screen and the clock does not stop, so the goal is steady, error-free typing rather than bursts of speed. Practise with light punctuation and everyday vocabulary — the passages are ordinary prose rather than technical text.
## Reaching the pass mark
Build your baseline with short daily sessions until you clear the required speed at 95%+ accuracy, then add a minute at a time to build stamina. Our government and bank typing pages cover the same clerical-test family; use them together for a rounded practice routine.
## What typing speed do SSC-type exams require?
Most SSC-type government exams set a qualifying bar around 30–35 WPM (or the KPH equivalent) with a cap on mistakes, tested as a short timed passage. For the full comparison across data entry, clerk, transcription and office roles — plus the WPM↔CPM↔KPH conversions — see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

## Why typing matters for teachers
Teaching involves a constant stream of typed work: lesson plans, schemes of work, reports, feedback and parent emails. Being a comfortable typist saves hours every week and leaves more energy for the classroom.
## What speed is expected
Teaching itself rarely sets a formal typing test, but the admin side rewards 45 WPM or more with good accuracy. Office-based education roles and school administrators often expect the same 40 to 55 WPM range as other admin jobs, and support-staff interviews may include a short timed test.
## Tools teachers use
Mark and feedback, online portals and shared documents all reward fast, accurate typing. Keeping accuracy high means fewer corrections in reports that others will read, which matters as much as speed.
## Practise in small gaps
You do not need a big block of time. A one-minute test between lessons, repeated daily, is enough to lift your speed steadily. Watch the accuracy figure and aim to hold it above 96% as your WPM rises.

## Keyboard Practice
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/keyboard-practice.html

Before speed comes familiarity. Practise finding every key without looking and build the habits that make fast typing possible.

## Start with the home row
Rest your left fingers on A, S, D, F and your right on J, K, L, ; — the home row. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so you can find them by touch. Every finger owns a column of keys and returns to the home row after each reach; that is the whole secret of touch typing.
## Practise, don't hunt
Hunting for keys with two fingers feels fast at first but caps your speed hard. Practising the correct finger for each key, even when it is slower to begin with, builds the muscle memory that makes fast typing automatic later.
## Use the on-screen keyboard
Turn on the virtual keyboard and the next-key highlight so you can see which finger should reach which key. The on-screen hand guide shows the correct finger for the letter you are about to type — follow it closely for the first few sessions.
## Little and often
Ten focused minutes a day beats one long weekly session. Keep accuracy above 97% and let speed rise on its own; rushing before the habits are set just trains mistakes. Return to this page whenever you want a clean, distraction-free practice space.
## Placement and finger training guides
Build the map correctly: typing finger chart for every key, and finger placement typing with per-finger drills.
## Kid-first keyboard practice
Turn keyboard drills into the game that lands: typing games for kids — letter-hunt, word-collection, and the 5-minute session template.
## Keyboard Practice FAQ
Start on the home row, use the correct finger for every key, and keep your eyes on the screen. Practise about ten focused minutes a day with instant feedback.
The home row is the middle letter row: A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right. F and J have raised bumps to guide your fingers.
No. Looking at the keyboard stops you building muscle memory. Use the on-screen keyboard and hand guide instead, and trust your fingers to learn.
Yes, free and no sign-up, on desktop and mobile.

## Japanese Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/japanese-typing-test.html

Test your Japanese typing speed with real Japanese sentences mixing kanji, hiragana and katakana. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

## Japanese typing test
A Japanese typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Japanese text — sentences that mix kanji, hiragana and katakana exactly the way everyday Japanese is written. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so the score stays comparable with the classic 1 minute typing test.
## Romaji input, kana input and the IME
Most people type Japanese with a romaji-to-kana IME: you type roman letters, the IME converts them to kana, and you confirm kanji conversions as you go. This test shows the finished Japanese sentence, so it trains the reading-and-confirming rhythm that real Japanese typing depends on, whichever input method you use.
## How to improve Japanese typing speed
Accuracy first: a missed kanji conversion costs far more time than a slow, clean sentence. Practise short daily rounds, keep your eyes on the screen, and let your fingers learn the romaji syllable rhythm — consonant plus vowel — that almost every Japanese word follows.
## WPM, CPM and Japanese
Because Japanese packs meaning into characters, one Japanese 'word' carries more content than one English word. Watch your characters per minute (CPM) alongside WPM: for Japanese, CPM is often the fairer measure of real input speed.
## Japanese typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Either works. The test shows real Japanese sentences; you reproduce the characters with your usual input method — romaji-to-kana IME, kana input, or a Japanese keyboard.

## Korean Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/korean-typing-test.html

Test your Korean typing speed with real Korean sentences in Hangul. Measure your speed and accuracy instantly with live results. Free, no sign up.

## Korean typing test
A Korean typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Korean sentences — everyday Hangul text with natural spacing (띄어쓰기) and punctuation. Your score appears in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so results stay comparable with the standard 1 minute typing test.
## Hangul syllable blocks and typing rhythm
Hangul is typed letter by letter — ㅎ, ㅏ, ㄴ — and the IME assembles each syllable block (한) as you go. That means Korean typing speed is really about how fast your fingers roll through the jamo inside each block. Smooth, even syllable rhythm beats short bursts of speed.
## How to improve Korean typing speed
Keep your fingers on the home row (ㅁㄴㅇㄹ / ㅏㅓㅣㅡ positions on the standard 2-set keyboard), look at the screen not the keyboard, and practise short daily rounds. Accuracy first: fixing a mis-composed syllable costs more time than typing it slowly and cleanly.
## WPM and CPM for Korean
Korean syllable blocks pack several letters into one character, so raw WPM understates the work your fingers do. Watch your characters per minute (CPM) as well: it tracks the real keystroke load of Korean text.
## Korean typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Any. The test shows real Korean sentences and measures what you produce, so the standard 2-set Hangul layout, 3-set layouts, or a mobile Korean keyboard all work.
You type individual jamo (letters) and the IME composes them into syllable blocks automatically. Fast Korean typing comes from an even jamo rhythm inside each block, not from rushing whole words.
Both are shown after each round. Because each Hangul block contains several letters, CPM (characters per minute) reflects your true keystroke speed better than WPM.
Yes. Timed sentence practice with real Hangul text builds the speed and accuracy measured in Korean office, civil-service and data-entry typing tests.

## Urdu Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/urdu-typing-test.html

Test your Urdu typing speed with real Urdu sentences in the Perso-Arabic script, typed right to left. Instant speed and accuracy results. Free, no sign up.

## Urdu typing test
An Urdu typing test measures how fast and accurately you type real Urdu sentences in the Perso-Arabic (Nastaliq-style) script, written and read right to left. Your result is shown in words per minute, where every 5 characters counts as one word, so you can compare scores with the classic typing test 1 minute round.
## Right-to-left typing: what changes
The cursor moves right to left, and letters change shape depending on their position in a word — initial, medial, final or isolated forms join automatically as you type. This test renders the practice text and your input right to left, exactly as Urdu appears in real documents, so what you practise is what you produce.
## How to improve Urdu typing speed
Practise with real sentences rather than single letters, keep your eyes on the screen, and slow down at first for the characters that sit above and below the line — the diacritics and the special letters ٹ ڈ ڑ ں ہ ے. Accuracy first: rasm (spelling) mistakes cost more time than a steady, clean pace.
## Urdu typing for exams and office work
Timed Urdu passage typing is the format used in Pakistani government, court and data-entry exams, usually set in InPage or standard Urdu keyboards. Daily timed rounds with real sentences build the same speed and accuracy those tests measure — and your CPM shows the raw keystroke rate alongside WPM.
## Urdu typing test FAQ
Yes. It is free with no sign up, and your practice history stays on your own device.
Yes. Both the practice text and your input field run right to left, the way real Urdu is written and read, so your practice matches real documents.

Yes. Timed sentence practice in the Perso-Arabic script is the standard format of Pakistani government and court typing tests, so daily rounds build the same measured speed and accuracy.

## Why drill the top English words
In almost every language, a few hundred words cover most of what people actually write. English is no exception: these 200 words appear again and again in messages, documents, subtitles and web pages. If your fingers can produce them without thinking, your real-world English typing speed rises immediately — long before you memorise any larger vocabulary.
English high-frequency words are mostly short function words (the, of, and) mixed with everyday verbs and nouns. They are the words where touch-typing muscle memory pays off fastest, because you type them thousands of times a day.
## How to practise English typing with this list
Start the test above — it draws words from this very list, so every round drills the words that matter. Type a short round every day, aim for accuracy first (97%+), and only then push for speed. Watch the weak-key report after each round: it shows exactly which letters slow you down, so you can target them instead of re-typing words you already know.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the English typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.

## Why drill the top Hindi words
In almost every language, a few hundred words cover most of what people actually write. Hindi is no exception: these 200 words appear again and again in messages, documents, subtitles and web pages. If your fingers can produce them without thinking, your real-world Hindi typing speed rises immediately — long before you memorise any larger vocabulary.
Hindi high-frequency words are rich in matras and the conjunct consonants (क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ) that slow most typists down. Drilling these 200 words builds automaticity exactly where Hindi typing needs it.
## How to practise Hindi typing with this list
Start the test above — it draws words from this very list, so every round drills the words that matter. Type a short round every day, aim for accuracy first (97%+), and only then push for speed. Watch the weak-key report after each round: it shows exactly which letters slow you down, so you can target them instead of re-typing words you already know.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the Hindi typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.

## Why drill the top Japanese words
In almost every language, a few hundred words cover most of what people actually write. Japanese is no exception: these 200 words appear again and again in messages, documents, subtitles and web pages. If your fingers can produce them without thinking, your real-world Japanese typing speed rises immediately — long before you memorise any larger vocabulary.
Japanese high-frequency words are dominated by particles (は, が, を, に) and the most common verbs and auxiliaries. Because Japanese has no spaces between words, learning to type these fragments instantly is what makes full-sentence typing feel fluent.
## How to practise Japanese typing with this list
Start the test above — it draws words from this very list, so every round drills the words that matter. Type a short round every day, aim for accuracy first (97%+), and only then push for speed. Watch the weak-key report after each round: it shows exactly which letters slow you down, so you can target them instead of re-typing words you already know.
When you want full sentences instead of single words, switch to the Japanese typing test, or benchmark yourself against the classic 1 minute typing test.

## Quotes typing test
A quotes typing test measures your speed and accuracy on real famous quotations — the same sentences people actually read, share and write. Unlike random word drills, quotes make you type the way real writing flows: natural word order, commas and full stops in the right places, and capital letters that mark where thoughts begin.
## Why quotes are the best typing practice text
Quotes are dense with the two things that slow most typists down: punctuation and capitals. Every sentence forces you to handle them at speed, which is exactly the skill that separates a fast prose typist from a fast word-list typist. And because the lines are memorable, your brain reads ahead while your fingers follow — the same look-ahead rhythm that professional typists rely on.
The pool on this page mixes short, punchy lines with longer reflective ones, so a one-minute round trains both burst speed and sustained rhythm. If you want a warm-up first, the quick brown fox typing test covers every letter of the alphabet in a single sentence.
## What is in this quote collection
Thirty-five lines from public-domain and widely attributed authors — Twain, Aristotle, Franklin, Lincoln, Edison, Einstein, Lao Tzu, Marcus Aurelius and more. Each one is typed exactly as commonly cited, with the author's name after a dash, so you also practise the dash-and-capital pattern that citations use.
## How to use quotes to raise your WPM
Take one minute a day. Type the quote as if you were writing it down for someone else to read: clean capitals, clean punctuation, no shortcuts. Watch the weak-key report after each round — most people discover a specific symbol (the comma, the dash, the shift key) that taxes every sentence they type. Drill that, and your prose speed jumps within a week.

## Pangram Typing Test
Source: https://typing.rerivo.com/pangram-typing-test.html

Practice typing with pangrams — sentences that contain every letter of the alphabet. From the famous quick brown fox to fifteen harder variations. Free, instant results.

## Pangram typing test
A pangram typing test trains every key on the keyboard in a single sentence. A pangram is a sentence that uses all 26 letters at least once, so a few rounds guarantee your fingers visit every corner of the layout — including the rare letters (q, z, x, j) that ordinary prose barely touches.
## Why the rare letters matter
Typing speed is capped by your slowest keys, not your fastest. Most people fly through e, t and a but stumble on q, z, x and j simply because daily typing rarely calls for them. Pangram drills force those keys into your muscle memory, and once the rare letters stop being events, your baseline speed on normal text rises too.
## The pangrams in this test
Sixteen pangrams in rising difficulty, starting with the classic quick brown fox — which has its own dedicated page with more variations — and moving to trickier constructions like 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow' and 'Mr Jock, TV quiz PhD, bags few lynx'. The harder ones mix capitals, punctuation and unusual words for a full-keyboard workout.
## How to practise with pangrams
Run a minute a day and watch the weak-key report. When a pangram round flags the same letters round after round, those are your true weak keys — drill them until they disappear from the report. Alternate between the easy pangrams for warm-up and the hard ones for a proper challenge.
